exam: What immediate step do you take in a patient with acute mono‑articular knee swelling and fever? — Perform joint aspiration to exclude septic arthritis before assuming viral cause.

How does the pattern of joint involvement help differentiate viral arthritis from rheumatoid arthritis? — Viral arthritis is usually symmetric, acute, and self‑limited; rheumatoid arthritis is chronic, erosive, and may have extra‑articular features.
A 30‑year‑old farmer presents with fever, rash, and polyarthritis after a mosquito bite. Which virus is most likely and what specific test confirms it? — Chikungunya; IgM serology.
Why are high‑dose steroids contraindicated in an undifferentiated acute arthritis? — They can mask infection signs and worsen septic arthritis.

In a resource‑limited hospital without synovial fluid analysis, how would you safely manage a patient with suspected viral arthritis? — Treat symptomatically, monitor CRP and fever, and arrange transfer if joint becomes markedly painful or systemic signs worsen.
Explain why parvovirus B19 arthritis is more common in adults than children. — Adults have a more robust immune response causing immune‑complex mediated joint inflammation.
When is antiviral therapy indicated in viral arthritis? — When the causative virus has a specific treatment, e.g., acyclovir for HSV, or when HIV‑related arthritis occurs in a patient not on ART.
ai.title: Viral Arthritis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute joint inflammation caused by viral infections, often self‑limiting but may mimic bacterial septic arthritis. Recognise patterns, use limited investigations, and manage supportively while ruling out serious mimics.

b: Common viruses: Chikungunya, Parvovirus B19, Hepatitis B/C, HIV, Dengue, Rubella, Zika
Typical onset: 1‑14 days after fever or rash
Self‑limited in >90% of immunocompetent patients
sections.p: Viral arthritis is joint pain and swelling that occurs during or shortly after a systemic viral infection. It is usually transient, affecting large joints symmetrically, and resolves within weeks.

b: Symmetric polyarthritis → viral; mono‑articular, warm, severe pain → septic
Associated rash, fever, lymphadenopathy suggest viral aetiology
Absence of high neutrophil count in synovial fluid argues against bacterial infection
sections.p: Distinguish viral from bacterial septic arthritis and from rheumatic diseases by history, pattern of joint involvement, and basic labs. In low‑resource settings, focus on clinical clues and simple tests.

b: Early exclusion of septic arthritis is the priority
In HIV or immunocompromised patients, viral arthritis may coexist with opportunistic infections
sections.p: Prompt identification prevents unnecessary antibiotics and invasive procedures, while ensuring septic arthritis is not missed—a life‑ and limb‑threatening emergency.
When joint aspiration is unavailable, rely on clinical pattern and basic labs; treat as septic until proven otherwise.

t.b: Is the effusion septic? → Gram stain/culture; neutrophils >50 % suggest bacterial, lymphocyte‑predominant suggests viral
Is there leukocytosis? → Marked neutrophilia supports bacterial infection; mild lymphocytosis or normal WBC fits viral

t.a: Serum viral serology (IgM) for suspected virus
t.b: Is a specific virus present? → Positive IgM confirms recent infection (e.g., Chikungunya, Parvovirus B19)
Is there underlying rheumatoid disease? → Positive tests suggest chronic autoimmune arthritis rather than acute viral

b: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for pain and inflammation – avoid in renal failure or active GI ulcer
Paracetamol for fever and mild pain – safe in most patients
Hydration and joint rest; physiotherapy after acute phase
If bacterial septic arthritis cannot be excluded, start empirical IV antibiotics and arrange urgent referral
sections.p: Treat the underlying virus when specific therapy exists; otherwise provide analgesia, rest, and monitor for complications.

b: Septic arthritis – usually mono‑articular, high fever, toxic appearance
Rheumatic fever – migratory arthritis, carditis, Jones criteria
Systemic lupus erythematosus – arthritis with malar rash, renal involvement
Gout/CPPD – mono‑articular, crystal‑induced, often podagra
sections.p: Conditions that present with acute polyarthritis.

b: CRP may be modest early in viral arthritis, falsely reassuring
Synovial fluid WBC can be <20 000 cells/µL in early septic arthritis
sections.p: Laboratory values that may be normal early in disease.

b: Always rule out septic arthritis first
Identify viral clues: rash, recent travel, vector exposure
Know which viruses have specific treatments (e.g., acyclovir for HSV arthritis, antiretrovirals for HIV)
Explain why steroids are avoided in acute viral arthritis without confirmed diagnosis
sections.p: Key points examiners love to test.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever >39 °C with a single swollen, hot joint
Rapidly progressive joint destruction or neurovascular compromise
Severe unexplained systemic illness (e.g., hypotension, confusion)
